methods.label: A vertical section and an oblique counterexample
methods.explanation:
The wording leaves open whether the pyramid is right, meaning that its apex is directly above the center of its base. We first make that extra assumption to compute the intended answer, then check whether the printed conditions force it.

Assume the pyramid is right. Equal distances to each pair of opposite, equally sloping faces force the hemisphere's center to be the square's center \(O\). Let \(P\) be the apex and \(Q\) the midpoint of a base edge. Write \(OQ=h>0\), so the base edge is \(2h\) and \(OP=6\).

The vertical section through \(P,O,Q\) contains a radius-\(2\) semicircle tangent to \(PQ\). Its radius to the tangency point is perpendicular to \(PQ\). Thus triangle \(OPQ\) has area both \(3h\), using its perpendicular legs, and \(PQ\), using base \(PQ\) and altitude \(2\). By the Pythagorean theorem,
\[
3h=PQ=\sqrt{36+h^2}.
\]
Both sides are positive, so squaring gives \(8h^2=36\). Taking the positive root yields
\[
2h=\boxed{3\sqrt2},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\) under the right-pyramid assumption.

However, the printed statement also permits the following oblique pyramid. Use coordinates \((x,y,z)\), with the base in \(z=0\), and define
\[
h=\frac{13}{6},\qquad c=\frac{\sqrt7}{18},\qquad u=9c=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}.
\]
Take the base square to have vertices \((\pm h,\pm h,0)\), the apex to be \((u,u,6)\), and the hemisphere's center to be \(S=(c,c,0)\). This pyramid has height \(6\) and base edge \(2h=13/3\).

The two lateral face planes adjoining the base edges \(x=h\) and \(x=-h\) are
\[
6x+(h-u)z=6h,
\qquad -6x+(h+u)z=6h.
\]
The other two have the same equations with \(y\) replacing \(x\). Each plane is parallel to the omitted coordinate direction, so its perpendicular distance from \(S\) is computed by the point-to-line distance formula in the corresponding vertical section.

Here \(u=9c\) and \(h^2-9c^2=9/2\), which give
\[
36+(h\mp u)^2=9(h\mp c)^2.
\]
Consequently the distances from \(S\) to the four planes are all
\[
\frac{6(h\mp c)}{\sqrt{36+(h\mp u)^2}}=2.
\]
The center lies on the inward side of each plane, so the radius-\(2\) sphere lies in all four inward half-spaces. Moreover, solving for the perpendicular feet gives their heights as
\[
z_{\pm}=\frac{6(h\mp c)(h\mp u)}{36+(h\mp u)^2}>0,
\]
since \(h>u>c>0\). Thus all four tangencies occur on the upper hemisphere and on the lateral faces. Its base disk fits strictly inside the square because
\[
h-c=\frac{39-\sqrt7}{18}>2.
\]
This verifies every printed condition for base edge \(\boxed{13/3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

Therefore the displayed conditions do not determine a unique answer. Choice A requires the additional right-pyramid condition, while choice B is also possible as written.
